questions.q: Which animal has the largest testicles on earth, at roughly 1,100 pounds each?
questions.note: Each one outweighs you and everybody you came here with.

questions.q: The Argentine lake duck holds the record for the longest penis of any bird. How long does it get?
questions.note: On a duck that is barely 16 inches long. Nature plays favorites.

questions.q: Relative to its own body size, which creature has the longest penis in the animal kingdom?
questions.note: Up to eight times its body length. It is cemented to a rock, so it has to reach.

questions.q: Female spotted hyenas are famous for giving birth through what?
questions.note: First-time hyena mothers often lose the first cub. The matriarchy has a brutal entry fee.

questions.q: Male honeybees that successfully mate with the queen experience what immediately afterward?
options: Their genitals rip off and they die
They lose the ability to fly
questions.note: He explodes mid-air and his junk stays behind as a plug. Best day and last day.

questions.q: What happens to the male deep-sea anglerfish when he finds a mate?
options: He fuses to her body permanently and becomes a sperm sac
He guards the eggs for a year
questions.note: His eyes and guts dissolve. He is now a testicle with a commute of zero.

questions.q: Kangaroos have how many vaginas?
questions.note: Two for incoming, one in the middle for outgoing. Infrastructure.

questions.q: The echidna has a penis with how many heads?
questions.note: Four heads, but only two work at a time, and it alternates sides. Australia again.

questions.q: Why do vultures deliberately urinate on their own legs?
options: To cool off and kill bacteria
questions.note: Pee as both air conditioning and hand sanitizer. Say what you want, it works.

questions.q: Hippos secrete a thick red fluid often called blood sweat. What does it actually do?
questions.note: A two-ton animal oozing its own SPF. You paid nineteen dollars for a tube.

questions.q: Wombat droppings are famously what shape?
questions.note: Cube-shaped so they do not roll off the rocks the wombat is marking. Precision pooping.

questions.q: The emerald cockroach wasp does what to a cockroach?
options: Eats it alive on the spot
Stings its brain, makes it docile, and walks it to a burrow to be eaten by larvae
Uses it to build a nest wall
questions.note: It leads the roach by the antenna like a dog on a leash. Hell is real and it is tiny.

questions.q: Cymothoa exigua, the tongue-eating louse, does what to its host fish?
options: Severs the tongue and takes its place
questions.note: The fish keeps living with a crustacean as its tongue. Think about that next time you order fish.

questions.q: Male antechinus, a small Australian marsupial, do what during their one breeding season?
options: Fight to the death over territory
Mate until their immune systems collapse and they die
questions.note: Two weeks of nonstop sex, then organ failure. He knew the deal going in.

questions.q: Ophiocordyceps fungus is known for doing what to ants?
options: Causing them to attack their own colony
Taking over their behavior, marching them up a stem, then erupting from their head
questions.note: Yes, this is where the zombie show got it. Nature wrote it first and did not need a budget.

questions.q: Naegleria fowleri, the brain-eating amoeba, usually enters a person how?
options: Up the nose in warm freshwater
questions.note: Swallowing it is fine. Snorting the lake is the problem. Keep your nose out of warm ponds.

questions.q: Roughly how many Demodex mites are living on the average adult human face right now?
questions.note: They live in your pores, eat your oil, and mate on your face while you sleep. Good night.

questions.q: When threatened, a sea cucumber may do what?
questions.note: It shoots its guts at you and grows new ones. Petty and effective.

questions.q: Pineapple makes your mouth sting because it contains an enzyme that does what?
options: Triggers a mild allergy in everyone
questions.note: Bromelain. You are eating the pineapple and the pineapple is eating you. Mutual.

questions.q: Castoreum, historically used as a vanilla-ish flavoring and fragrance, comes from what?
options: Beaver castor sacs near the anus
questions.note: Barely used in food anymore because milking a beaver is expensive and insane.

questions.q: Ambergris, long prized by perfumers, is what?
options: A waxy substance from sperm whale intestines
questions.note: Whale gut rock that washes up on beaches. People have paid six figures for it.

questions.q: Carmine, the red food coloring, is made from what?
questions.note: Thousands of bugs per pound. That strawberry yogurt has a body count.

questions.q: Casu marzu, a Sardinian cheese, is distinguished by what?
options: It is made from donkey milk
It is aged in a cave for 20 years
questions.note: The maggots can jump six inches, so people eat it with their eyes shielded. Dinner and a show.

questions.q: Hakarl, the Icelandic delicacy, is made by fermenting what?
questions.note: Greenland shark meat is toxic fresh, so they bury it until it is merely horrifying.

questions.q: Surstromming, the Swedish fermented herring, is notable for being what?
options: Smelly enough that some airlines refuse to carry it
The most expensive fish in Europe
questions.note: The cans bulge from internal pressure. Open it outdoors or lose your security deposit.

questions.q: The corpse flower smells like rotting meat in order to attract what?
options: Nothing, it is a side effect
questions.note: It spends up to a decade building up to one weekend of smelling like a dead body. Relatable.

questions.q: The gympie-gympie, one of the most painful plants on earth, grows where?
questions.note: The sting can flare for months and the hairs survive in dried specimens for a century. Australia stays undefeated.

questions.q: The strongest commercially sold spirit, Polish Spirytus Rektyfikowany, is what proof?
questions.note: Ninety-six percent alcohol. It is not a drink, it is a dare with a tax stamp.

questions.q: What does the alcohol term proof originally come from?
options: A British navy test where spirit-soaked gunpowder was lit
questions.note: If the gunpowder still burned, the rum was proved. Sailors invented quality control with fire.

questions.q: The nasty part of a hangover is largely caused by which byproduct of alcohol metabolism?
questions.note: Your liver turns booze into something more toxic than booze before finishing the job. Thanks, liver.

questions.q: Methanol in badly made moonshine is dangerous because the body turns it into what?
questions.note: Blindness is the famous outcome. Buy your liquor from people with a license and a lawyer.

questions.q: The hallucinogenic reputation of absinthe comes from thujone. What does the science actually say?
options: Absinthe contains far too little thujone to do anything
questions.note: The green fairy was just 140 proof. People were obliterated, not enlightened.

questions.q: Albert Hofmann accidentally dosed himself with LSD and rode his bicycle home on which date, now celebrated as Bicycle Day?
questions.note: The worst commute in the history of chemistry.

questions.q: MDMA was first synthesized and patented by which company, decades before anyone took it recreationally?
questions.note: Patented in 1912 and then ignored for sixty years. Worst product launch ever, best eventual word of mouth.

questions.q: Ketamine was originally developed and is still widely used as what?
options: An anesthetic, including in veterinary medicine
questions.note: Yes, the horse thing is real, and no, that is not why it is in the clinic.

questions.q: Nitrous oxide was being used recreationally at upper-class parties as early as when?
questions.note: Humphry Davy threw laughing gas parties for poets. Nothing is new, including your Saturday.

questions.q: Amyl nitrite, better known as poppers, was originally prescribed for what?
questions.note: A heart drug that found a second career. Happens to the best of us.

questions.q: Viagra was originally being developed to treat what?
questions.note: The trial participants kept declining to return their leftover pills. Data is data.

questions.q: Minoxidil, sold as a hair-regrowth treatment, started out as what?
questions.note: Patients grew hair in places they did not ask about. Somebody in marketing had a very good day.

questions.q: Caffeine's estimated lethal dose for an adult works out to roughly how much brewed coffee?
questions.note: Your bladder files for divorce around cup nine, so you are statistically safe.

questions.q: Nicotine's original industrial use was as what?
questions.note: You are smoking bug spray with a filter on it.

questions.q: A 2022 study counted the nerve fibers in the human clitoris for the first time. Roughly how many did it find?
questions.note: More than 10,000, which is roughly double the old textbook guess. Textbooks were written by guys who did not check.

questions.q: A 2015 review of 17 studies put the average erect human penis length at about what?
questions.note: 13.1 centimeters. Everyone in this room just did math.

questions.q: A study of penile fracture injuries found which sex position was involved most often?
questions.note: Woman-on-top came out on top, so to speak. There is a whole body of urology literature on this.

questions.q: Semen is made up of sperm plus fluid. Roughly what percentage is actual sperm?
questions.note: The rest is sugar, enzymes and transport fluid. Mostly packaging, like everything else.

questions.q: The medical term for an erection that will not go away and requires emergency care is what?
questions.note: Named after Priapus, a Greek god with a famously permanent situation. Four hours and you call someone.

questions.q: Which of these is true about the human G-spot?
options: There is no agreed-upon distinct structure; it is likely part of the internal clitoral network
It was removed from medical texts in 1970
It only exists in about half of people
It is a distinct anatomical organ confirmed by dissection
questions.note: Decades of searching and nobody has produced the thing. The clitoris is just bigger than advertised.

questions.q: The widely repeated story that Victorian doctors invented the vibrator to treat female hysteria is what?
options: Largely unsupported by evidence and traced to one poorly sourced book
questions.note: A 2018 review tore it apart. Great movie premise, bad history.

questions.q: Which animal, besides humans, is well documented to have sex for pleasure and use it socially?
questions.note: Bonobos resolve basically every conflict this way. World peace is one strategy away.

questions.q: The clitoris and penis develop from which embryonic structure?
options: The same structure, the genital tubercle
questions.note: Same raw material, different final assembly. We are all working from one blueprint.

questions.q: Nocturnal erections, sometimes called morning wood, happen roughly how often per night in healthy adult males?
questions.note: It is tied to REM sleep. Your body is just doing maintenance checks.

questions.q: In 897, the Catholic Church held the Cadaver Synod, in which a dead pope was what?
options: Exhumed, dressed in robes, and put on trial
questions.note: They propped up the corpse and assigned a deacon to answer for it. Guilty, obviously.

questions.q: Napoleon's preserved penis has reportedly done what since his death?
options: Been sold at auction more than once and ended up in a New Jersey collection
questions.note: Allegedly removed during the autopsy. The provenance is murky but the auction records are not.

questions.q: Abraham Lincoln's coffin was reportedly opened or moved roughly how many times after his funeral?
questions.note: Grave robbers, relocations and anxious officials checking he was still in there. Let the man rest.

questions.q: In 1518 Strasbourg, dozens of people were struck by what strange affliction?
options: Compulsive dancing that went on for weeks
questions.note: Some reportedly danced until they collapsed. Authorities responded by hiring musicians. Bold call.

questions.q: Astronomer Tycho Brahe died shortly after a banquet, reportedly from what?
options: A bladder or kidney problem after refusing to leave the table to urinate
questions.note: Too polite to pee. Modern tests ruled out the mercury poisoning theory.

questions.q: Tycho Brahe also famously wore a prosthetic nose. Why?
options: He lost the original in a sword duel over a math argument
questions.note: A duel. Over mathematics. With his cousin. Peak sixteenth century.

questions.q: Mummy brown, a real Victorian artist's pigment, was made from what?
questions.note: Painters stopped using it when they realized what was in the tube. Some took a while.

questions.q: Scheele's green, a wildly popular Victorian wallpaper color, was dangerous because it contained what?
questions.note: People slowly poisoned themselves because the drawing room looked fantastic. Priorities.

questions.q: Eben Byers, a wealthy American, died in 1932 after years of drinking what?
options: Radium-infused water sold as a health drink
questions.note: He drank roughly 1,400 bottles. His jaw and skull deteriorated. The product was called Radithor.

questions.q: The Great Stink of 1858 finally forced London to build proper sewers because the smell did what?
options: Overwhelmed Parliament, sitting right on the Thames
Killed a thousand people in a week
questions.note: Nothing motivates legislators like the problem reaching their own windows.

questions.q: Bayer trademarked and marketed heroin in 1898 as what?
questions.note: Sold over the counter alongside aspirin. One of those became the problem child.

questions.q: Vin Mariani, a nineteenth-century cocaine-laced wine, famously received an endorsement from whom?
questions.note: He reportedly carried a hip flask of it and gave the company a gold medal. Blessed be the dose.

questions.q: The 1919 Boston Molasses Disaster killed how many people?
options: Nobody, it was property damage only
questions.note: A wave of molasses moving around 35 miles an hour. The harbor reportedly smelled sweet for years.

questions.q: Mike the Headless Chicken survived for roughly how long after losing his head in 1945?
questions.note: The axe missed the brain stem. He was fed with a dropper and toured the country.

questions.q: Which one-man wrecking crew invented both leaded gasoline and chlorofluorocarbons?
questions.note: Two world-scale environmental disasters, one resume. He has been called the most destructive organism in history.

questions.q: Ozzy Osbourne bit the head off a bat onstage in 1982 and then had to get what?
questions.note: He thought it was rubber. It was not rubber.

questions.q: Honey essentially does not spoil. Why?
options: Low water content, acidity and bee-made peroxide block microbes
Bees add a natural preservative salt
It is simply too sweet for bacteria to notice
questions.note: The famous edible-tomb-honey story is thinly sourced, but the chemistry is real. Honey does not spoil, it just gets smug.

questions.q: The record for longest documented time a person has gone without sleep, set in 1964, is about what?
questions.note: 264 hours. By the end he was hallucinating and failing basic math. Guinness stopped accepting attempts.

questions.q: Joey Chestnut's record for hot dogs and buns eaten in 10 minutes stands at what?
questions.note: Seventy-six. Set in 2021. Do not think about the hours afterward.

questions.q: A fart is flammable mainly because of which gases?
questions.note: Hydrogen sulfide does the smelling, hydrogen and methane do the burning. Different departments.

questions.q: Not everybody's gut produces methane. Roughly what share of people are methane producers?
options: Somewhere between a third and half
questions.note: Estimates vary by population, but plenty of people make none at all. So only some of you can be lit on fire.

questions.q: Which of these is actually in the top tier of strongest known natural poisons by weight?
questions.note: And people pay to have small amounts injected into their foreheads. Context is everything.

questions.q: Mount Everest has a growing problem with what, enough that climbers are now required to pack it out?
questions.note: Decades of accumulated human waste on a frozen mountain. The view is still nice.

questions.q: The Icelandic Phallological Museum in Reykjavik collects what?
questions.note: Over two hundred specimens, including human donations. Tourism is a broad church.

questions.q: What was Listerine aggressively marketed as before it was mouthwash?
options: A floor cleaner and surgical antiseptic
questions.note: They basically invented the idea that bad breath was a social emergency, then sold the cure.

questions.q: Beer goggles have been studied scientifically. What do the better studies generally find?
options: A huge effect on perceived attractiveness
A modest effect, with bigger effects on confidence and willingness to approach
questions.note: Alcohol does not fix their face, it fixes your judgment about approaching it.

questions.q: What does alcohol do to your sleep?
options: Only affects REM in heavy drinkers
Deepens it across the whole night
Knocks you out faster but wrecks the second half of the night
questions.note: You pass out quickly and then wake at 4 a.m. staring at the ceiling, reviewing your decisions.

questions.q: Hangovers get worse with age mainly because of what?
options: A mix of slower metabolism, less water in the body, and worse sleep
questions.note: It is not one thing. It is everything, slowly, at once. Enjoy your thirties.

questions.q: Which of these drinks is most likely to give you a worse hangover at the same alcohol dose?
questions.note: Darker spirits carry more congeners. The brown stuff tastes better and charges interest.

questions.q: Bayer marketed heroin as a non-addictive substitute for morphine and sold it as a remedy for what?
questions.note: Bayer sold it as a cough medicine from 1898. Turned out it had one of the highest addiction rates of anything they ever bottled.

questions.q: The Great Molasses Flood of 1919 killed 21 people in Boston's North End. How fast was the molasses wave estimated to be moving?
questions.note: Around 35 mph. People were killed by syrup moving faster than the cars of the day.

questions.q: Pittsburgh industrialist Eben Byers drank roughly 1,400 bottles of a radium tonic called Radithor. What eventually had to be removed?
options: Most of his upper and lower jaw
questions.note: Most of his jaw. He was buried in a lead-lined coffin in 1932, and he is still radioactive.

questions.q: In 1848 a tamping iron blew through Phineas Gage's skull behind his left eye. How long did he live afterward?
questions.note: He died in 1860, nearly 12 years later. He kept working, and he kept the iron.

questions.q: Mike the Headless Chicken of Fruita, Colorado survived decapitation in 1945. For how long?
questions.note: About 18 months. The axe missed the jugular and most of the brain stem. He was fed with an eyedropper.

questions.q: Henry Ford built a rubber-plantation company town in the Brazilian Amazon in 1928. What sparked the 1930 worker revolt there?
questions.note: The cafeteria. Ford imposed oatmeal, brown rice and canned peaches on Amazonian laborers, and they drove the managers into the jungle.

questions.q: The London Beer Flood of 1814 released a wave of porter into the St Giles slum. How many people died?
questions.note: Eight, five of them mourners at a wake. The inquest ruled it an act of misfortune and the brewery paid nothing.

questions.q: King Mithridates VI spent years taking small doses of poison to build immunity. How did that work out when he tried to poison himself?
options: It failed and he needed a sword
questions.note: It failed. By Appian's account he had to ask his bodyguard to finish the job with a blade.

questions.q: Typhoid Mary spent about 26 years in forced quarantine. What got her locked up the second time?
options: Cooking at a maternity hospital under a fake name
questions.note: She took a job as a hospital cook calling herself Mary Brown, and started another outbreak.

questions.q: In the 1518 dancing plague of Strasbourg, dozens of people danced uncontrollably for weeks. What did the city authorities first try?
options: Hiring musicians to play for them
questions.note: They brought in musicians and a guildhall, on the theory that the dancers needed to dance it out. It did not help.

questions.q: Outlaw Elmer McCurdy's mummified corpse was found in 1976 hanging in a California funhouse. Who found it?
options: A TV crew filming an episode
questions.note: A crew filming The Six Million Dollar Man. A prop man moved what he thought was a dummy and its arm came off.

questions.q: Cocaine was removed from Coca-Cola in 1903. What does the company reportedly still import coca leaves for?
options: Spent, cocaine-free leaf as a flavoring
questions.note: Spent leaf. A New Jersey plant strips the cocaine for pharmaceutical use and the leftovers reportedly still go into the syrup.

questions.q: Trepanation, drilling a hole in a living skull, is among the oldest known surgeries. How far back does the archaeological evidence go?
questions.note: Seven to ten thousand years. At one French site, 40 of 120 skulls had holes, and many show signs of healing.

questions.q: Walter Freeman performed or supervised more than 3,500 transorbital lobotomies. What was his original instrument?
options: An ice pick from his kitchen
questions.note: A kitchen ice pick. He also toured hospitals in a customized van the press later called the lobotomobile.

questions.q: Thalidomide caused severe birth defects in an estimated 10,000 to 20,000 babies. What was it sold to treat?
questions.note: It was a sedative pitched to pregnant women for morning sickness. Roughly 40 percent of affected infants died at or shortly after birth.

questions.q: Pervitin, issued widely to German forces starting in 1938, was which drug?
questions.note: Methamphetamine, in tablet form. The withdrawal was bad enough that the army started cutting back by 1940.

questions.q: The beef tapeworm, Taenia saginata, can live about 25 years in a human. How long can one get?
questions.note: Usually 4 to 10 meters. Specimens over 22 meters have been reported, which is longer than a school bus.

questions.q: The Demodex mites living in the pores of most adult human faces do what at night?
options: Crawl out and mate on your skin
questions.note: They come out in the dark to mate on your face, then crawl back into your pores before morning.

questions.q: In 1858 the Thames got so foul that Parliament rushed through a sewer bill. What finally forced their hand?
options: The smell reaching their own chamber
A cholera outbreak in the Commons
questions.note: The stench. They had ignored it for years, then passed a 3 million pound sewer bill in 18 days once it reached their windows.

questions.q: In the 1618 Defenestration of Prague, three men were thrown about 70 feet from a window. What happened to them?
options: They were caught in a net
questions.note: All three lived. Catholics credited angels, and Protestant pamphleteers later claimed they landed in a dung heap.

questions.q: Charles Osborne holds the record for the longest attack of hiccups. How long did it last?
questions.note: Sixty-eight years, from 1922 to 1990, estimated at 430 million hiccups. They stopped on their own a year before he died.

questions.q: The corpse flower, Amorphophallus titanum, stinks of rotting meat. How far away can the smell be detected?
questions.note: Up to half a mile. The blend includes compounds that smell like feces, rotting fish and sweaty socks, and it peaks at night.

questions.q: The Donner Party set out with 87 members in 1846. How many survived?
questions.note: Forty-eight. Some ate the dead, and two Miwok guides were murdered and eaten.

questions.q: The Radium Girls got radiation poisoning at a New Jersey watch-dial factory. How was the radium getting into them?
options: They pointed the brushes with their lips
It was in the drinking water
questions.note: They put the brushes in their mouths to shape the tips. Some painted their teeth with it for fun on dates.

questions.q: Tollund Man, a bog body from around 400 BCE, was so well preserved researchers identified his last meal. What was it?
questions.note: Barley porridge with seeds and a bit of fish, eaten 12 to 24 hours before he was hanged. His stubble and eyelashes survived too.

questions.q: In parts of Britain and Ireland, a "sin-eater" was paid to do what at a funeral?
options: Eat bread and ale over the corpse
questions.note: Eat a meal off or over the body to absorb the dead person's sins. The pay was lousy and the job made you an outcast.

questions.q: Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome causes relentless vomiting. What famously relieves it?
questions.note: Scalding hot showers, so reliably that compulsive bathing is treated as a diagnostic clue. Some patients burn themselves doing it.

questions.q: The "wick effect" is the natural explanation for bodies that burn almost completely in otherwise undamaged rooms. What acts as the wick?
options: Charred clothing soaked in body fat
questions.note: Burned clothing wicks up melted subcutaneous fat and keeps the body burning like a candle for hours. It has been tested with pig tissue.

questions.q: Sarah Winchester's bizarre San Jose mansion has stairs that go nowhere and doors opening onto walls. What actually explains most of it?
questions.note: The 1906 earthquake plus 22 years of unplanned additions. The ghost story came later and sells better.

questions.q: What is the medical term for a stomach rumble?
questions.note: Borborygmus. It is just gas and fluid being squeezed through your intestines, and it has nothing to do with being hungry.
